state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Alternate angles are actually a type of pair of angles formed when a transversal intersects two lines. They are always equal in measure, but not all angles in a figure are equal. In the case of angles \( p \) and \( q \), they are indeed alternate angles, so Tom is correct in this scenario. Can you explain why alternate angles are always equal in measure?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so you're saying Tom is right because p and q are alternate angles? But I'm confused - you said alternate angles are always equal, so why isn't Katie also right? And does that mean alternate angles are only equal when the two lines are parallel, or are they always equal no matter what?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Yes, Tom is correct because angles \(p\) and \(q\) are indeed alternate angles. Alternate angles are always equal, but they are only formed when a transversal intersects two lines. They do not have to be formed by parallel lines. Can you think of any other examples where you can identify alternate angles?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher makes a critical mathematical error by stating that alternate angles are always equal regardless of whether lines are parallel, directly reinforcing rather than correcting the student's misconception, and the student's Turn 2 response shows increased confusion rather than improvement.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts direct explanation, they provide incorrect mathematical information (claiming alternate angles don't require parallel lines and are always equal regardless of line configuration), which fundamentally violates the clarity and accuracy expected in traditional instruction.
